review:
"Kenji Eno, creator of 'D', got a fake 'clean' version of the game approved before deliberately submitting the master late, knowing the delay would force him to hand-deliver it to manufacturers in the US. On the plane, he switched the 'clean' discs with the real discs, bypassing all censorship."

Único jogo do Kenji Eno que eu joguei, não sei quando vou entrar em contato com os próximos. Feliz por finalmente ter conseguido jogar algo desse artista que eu sempre me interessei.

Se você está esperando um jogo de terror tradicional, com ação, sustos constantes ou mecânicas modernas… D: The Game não é isso — e ainda bem.

 Esse é um daqueles títulos raros que parecem mais um experimento artístico do que um jogo convencional. A experiência é lenta, quase sufocante, com uma atmosfera pesada que vai crescendo aos poucos. Há pouco combate, não há interface cheia de informações — só você, o ambiente e uma sensação constante de que algo está muito errado.

 Outro ponto interessante é a ausência de salvamento fácil. Isso aumenta a tensão e faz cada decisão importar mais, algo raro hoje em dia. Pode frustrar alguns jogadores, mas também torna a experiência mais memorável.

 Visualmente, considerando a época, o uso de FMV (Full Motion Video) e gráficos pré-renderizados cria um clima único, quase onírico. Já a trilha sonora é minimalista, muitas vezes substituída por silêncio — o que só deixa tudo mais inquietante.

 Não é um jogo para todos. Mas se você gosta de experiências diferentes, narrativas estranhas e daquele tipo de terror mais psicológico e experimental, vale muito a pena.

 Descanse em paz, Kenji Eno.

Back before Windows 98 was released, my family finally got their first PC from some shady shop that disappeared as quickly as it popped up. The PC came with a beta version of Windows 98 and some hacked games like Diablo and Carmageddon. We went shopping shortly after and picked up a few CD-ROM games: Ultimate Doom, Shivers II, Prisoner of Ice, Myst, and D.

At the time, the graphics of D blew me away. It was like playing a movie! I played through it many times, got my girlfriend to play it, etc. I did get D2 on Dreamcast but didn't like it as much and didn't play it for long. It fell to the back of my memories until recently, when scrolling through my Steam library and seeing it in there. I loaded it up and let my 13-year-old son give it a go.

He played through twice; first time he ran out of time (like we all do), but he stuck with it and did well - until the last decision, when he got the bad ending. He gave up after that, but overall enjoyed his time with it. Surprising, but he does appreciate all sorts of retro games.

Anyhow, thanks for keeping this game alive. And thanks to Valve and co. for letting it run on Linux, as I switched back in 2002.

One chilling night...

You receive a phone call from the police about your father, Dr. Harris. A once renowned & well respected Doctor & Director of the L.A National Hospital, now a mass murdering psychopath who locked himself away within it. Rushing all the way from San Francisco, [b]you[/b], Laura Harris, make your way onto the tragic crime scene, as you try and figure out just what the hell happened and why your father would commit such heinous crimes.

[b]This game is a classic[/b]. Originally released for the Panasonic 3DO, D is an old school, fully CGI, FMV, murder mystery, spookathon, with a twist. That twist being that as soon as you pop in the disc (or...boot up the game in this case) you have 2 hours to complete the entire ordeal before things get even worse for poor-ole Laura. No saving, no pausing, just [b]you[/b] and the chillingly, charming, atmosphere, this 1995 FMV game has to offer. In D, what you see is quite literally what you get, a short but interesting experience, that at the time, was really like no other. Whether or not that [b]still[/b] holds up in today's view is...really up to the individual. I wont pretend D is some sort of "hidden gem" that needs to be played and experience by everyone out there. But it [b]is[/b] a historic piece of gaming history and has something...truly alluring about it. Sure its slow, its a bit clunky, and for a horror game is not really all that scary, lol. But there's something...just so enigmatic and mysterious about this game, and that same something has had me come back to it time and time again. If old school point & clicks are your thing, or you just happen to have an insatiable curiosity for the horror genre and its earlier roots, D is one that does things juuust bizarrely enough to warrant at least a glance at. 

I love this game, and if you decide to pull the trigger, I hope you find something to love about it too.

D é um jogo de terror e quebra-cabeça no qual você controla a filha de um assassino em massa enquanto tenta achar o seu pai e descobrir o que levou ele a fazer isso. Ele funciona basicamente como um jogo adventure/point-and-click em primeira pessoa, com o jogador usando as setas, inventário e um botão de ação para se locomover pelas diferentes cenas FMV do jogo e interagir com o cenário, mas com um diferencial: o jogo possui um timer de 2 horas, e o jogador deve terminar o jogo dentro deste limite em apenas uma sessão para ver o seu final.

Esse é certamente um produto de seu tempo: seus visuais, que para a época eram tão impressionantes que o modelo 3D da personagem principal era considerado pela equipe como uma "atriz digital" que protagonizou vários de seus jogos, hoje em dia são considerados bem simples e antiquados; e seus elementos de terror, que tiveram de ser contrabandeados pelo diretor do jogo no lançamento para contornar a censura da época, são leves quando comparados com o que temos hoje. Os sustos que o jogo tenta dar são risíveis, e a história presente aqui é completamente ilógica e absurda - se você for jogar, tente não tomar spoilers do que o D do título significa, é uma surpresa e tanto.

Mas para quem gosta de jogos antigos e com valor histórico, que é paciente e consegue se botar no lugar de alguém que jogaria ele no lançamento em 1995, certamente existe bastante a ser apreciado aqui. Mesmo que o 3D do jogo seja rudimentar, a direção das cutscenes e o posicionamento de câmera conseguem ser bem bons. E quanto ao seu enredo, vi outra análise comparar esse jogo com filmes de terror italianos dos anos 70 e 80, e essa comparação certamente se aplica: assim como esses filmes, o jogo se preocupa muito menos em coerência narrativa, e mais na criação de atmosfera e no aspecto visual da obra (para a época). Mesmo que vários de seus elementos sejam absurdos para os nossos padrões atuais, eles ainda assim contribuem para a construção da "vibe" da obra, se é que isso faz algum sentido.

Se o paragrafo acima te interessou, eu recomendo D. É uma experiência curta, sendo fácil terminar ele dentro do tempo limite de duas horas mesmo sem saber o que fazer, e eu acho que pessoas que apreciam jogos e filmes de terror antigos vão encontrar elementos que agradem elas aqui.

Out of the deep respect and inspiration I had for [i]Kenji Eno[/i] and his works, I had to write a review immediately after finishing the game. He was an iconoclast unafraid to stand against major corporations like Sony (!) back in his day, as a result only [i]D (1995)[/i] is currently accessible via official modern gaming platforms. Even D is the only project that is currently accessible, Eno also created several other renowned projects such as [i] D2 //or under its very Nippon title, Dの食卓2// Enemy Zero, and Real Sound: Kaze no Regret[/i] too. Although he left us at a very young age, he was an unorthodox visionary not only in the world of games, but also in music, visual arts, and technology as well who also pushed boundaries for the new techniques to gain traction in the gaming industry. His works are still remembered with respect by many influential figures across both music and gaming scenes, including names like [i]Hiroshi Yoshimura, Yūya Asaoka,[/i] and [i]Hideo Kojima[/i] (cf. [i]Memories of Kenji Eno, 2023[/i]).

Disclaimer: Sure, if you're even slightly familiar with horror genres, you’ll likely anticipate the plot twist very early on. But if you have a soft spot for platforms like the 3DO or MS-DOS, D might deserve your time for its atmosphere alone, especially considering how little time the game actually takes as it runs on a real-time countdown and must be completed within two hours of total, while still being able to deliver quite an experience for any techno-nostalgist.

If you'd like to better understand just how much of an ambience craftsman [i]Eno-san[/i] was and how seriously he took sensory experience as part of his design, here’s bit of a trivia for the interested: in 1997, while he was still working under [i]Warp[/i], he created [i]Real Sound: Kaze no Regret[/i], which was a project built around the experience of visually impaired players which forgoes visual representation almost entirely and manages to create an intersensory connection using what we now call spatial sound design. [i]Kínēma![/i]

[h1]By punks, for punks![/h1]
[b]Important disclaimer[/b]
[i]I never played or experienced [b]D[/b] before.
I knew the game's reputation, its creator, but that's it.
What you're reading here is certified 100% free of nostalgia goggles.[/i]

[h3]Let’s kick things off with some trivia that’s just too good to ignore.[/h3]
[b]D[/b] deals with subjects that were highly controversial for its time in the gaming world: violence, gore, cannibalism… Fully aware that the game wouldn’t pass censorship, Kenji Eno [i]deliberately[/i] sent his publisher a “safe” version of the game for approval, long past the deadline.
Once approved, and since they were running late, Eno was tasked with personally delivering the master copy to the manufacturing plant in the United States.
But instead, during his flight, he discreetly got rid of the approved version and replaced it with the full uncensored version he had originally made.

It might sound amusing, but in the name of artistic freedom, the man willingly risked his career, reputation, and major legal action from several parties, in a country not exactly known for its tolerance of disobedience.

Mad Motherfuc*er right there.

Luckily for him, the game was a massive commercial success in Japan (over a million copies sold), and it seems this story ended well for everyone involved...

[h3]Now let’s talk about the game![/h3]
The player controls Laura, daughter of a respected doctor.
One night, she learns her father has gone insane, barricaded himself in the hospital he runs, taken several people hostage, and murdered a large part of the staff in cold blood. She rushes to the scene, but once there, she’s suddenly teleported into a medieval castle - greeted by the corpses of prisoners, deadly traps, and other lovely surprises…
Laura must do her best to survive the place, and try to save her father by understanding what drove him to such madness.

It’s [i]mandatory[/i] to put this game in its proper historical context to really appreciate it: [b]D[/b] came out at a time when 3D was booming and everyone had their eyes on the latest graphical advancements.
Everything had to be in 3D to catch players’ attention and push the boundaries of “realism.”
Real-time rendering like that of high-end workstations wasn’t possible on consoles, but CD-ROMs were perfect for displaying video.

[b]D[/b] is therefore an adventure game made entirely of FMV (Full-Motion Video) - pre-rendered sequences recorded on professional machines able to render cutting-edge 3D environments, allowing players to enjoy what was, at the time, a stunning and realistic visual experience.
30 years later, let’s be honest, it has aged like warm milk.
With video compression added on top, [b]D[/b] has withered like a sunflower in the rain and has nothing left to boast about on the visual front.

Controls are as barebones as it gets: arrow keys to move, “I” to check your inventory, and spacebar to interact.
That’s it.
The game didn’t shine for its gameplay even back then, and nowadays it’s downright sluggish and painfully slow.
Every movement triggers a new video segment, showing Laura moving at a snail’s pace through these dark corridors.
On the bright side, it gives you time to make a coffee between scenes to stay awake.

As for progression, the game relies on typical survival-horror puzzles: a key here, a trap to disarm there, a color combination here, a tool to use there... Nothing mind-blowing.
The game has one major condition for completion: you must escape the castle in under two hours, video transitions and inventory management included.
It might sound [i]very[/i] short, but… well, the game is.
I had never played it before, and I got the best ending on my first try without a guide in 1 hour 45 minutes.
And I got lost more than a few times, but clearly, the time limit fits the extremely short runtime.

[h3]Doesn’t sound too great, huh? And yet...[/h3]
...Once in the right mindset, I found myself quite engaged.
[b]D[/b] is incredibly dated by today’s standards, and it’s unlikely to appeal to a younger audience - it offers little interest in terms of gameplay, gore, or puzzles.

But two kinds of people might still appreciate what [b]D[/b] has to offer: video game “historians” able to place a work in its proper context, and… fans of genre cinema, especially Italian horror.

Very clearly, [b]D[/b] could have been directed by Dario Argento, Lucio Fulci, or Michele Soavi and no one would bat an eye. The game shows no signs of its Japanese origins; it bathes in that surreal, strange, and occasionally clumsy atmosphere found in Italian cult classics like [b]Phenomena[/b], [b]The Sect (La Setta)[/b], or [b]The Beyond (L’Aldilà)[/b]... everything reeks of graphic violence, a desire to shock, and bold ideas executed with limited means, even if it sometimes falls flat or ends up looking a bit silly.

The sound design reinforces that impression, with subtle but effective tracks composed by Kenji Eno himself.
It’s occasionally hilarious: opening a plain old door with a suspenseful and overly dramatic music cue is a guilty pleasure that always brought a smile to my face. These are clichés I know all too well… and never tire of.

Don’t believe me?
The ending credits for the “good” ending are backed by a Heavy Metal track (with Kenji Eno on guitar) that’s way too cool to only show up once.
I wasn’t kidding - those directors’ influence runs deep in [b]D[/b].

Not much else to say about this classic, forgotten for valid reasons, remembered for many others.
If you’re not a die-hard fan of gaming history or '70s/'80s Italian cinema, odds are you won’t get much out of it.
But if you see yourself in that description…
You’re in for a unique title with a strong personality. 

Flawed, but full of heart. 
Revolutionary in its time, and well worth knowing... if only for the culture.

Thank you, Mr. Eno, the most punk game designer of his era!

첫출시가 1995년도인데, 그 당시에 소니가 3D 기술로 서드 파티한테 어필하던 시기니까 그래픽이 나름 괜찮지 않나 싶다. 그래픽 뿐만 아니라 주인공 로라의 모델링도 좋고, 상호작용을 통한 컷씬에서 캐릭터가 큰 어색함 없이 잘 움직인다.

게임 시스템적으로 독특한 것은 2시간 안에 깨야한다는 것, 세이브 지원을 안해서 게임 시작하면 무조건 깨야되고, 2시간이 딱 되면 다시 하라고 문구가 뜨고 게임이 꺼진다... 아이템 창에 있는 시계로 시간은 계속 체크 가능하다. 3시에서 5시까지.

1인칭 3D 어드벤처 장르로 내가 해본 다른 비슷한 게임들(미스트, 살람보, 드라큘라, 미스테리어스 아일랜드 등)과 비교하면 난이도는 정말 쉽다. 2시간 안에 클리어해야 하는 특성상 게임의 분량 자체가 적다. 그리고 위의 게임들과 달리 맵이 저택?의 내부고, 돌아다닐 공간 자체가 크지 않다. 아이템은 멀리서 조달하거나 조합을 하는 시스템도 없어서 얻으면 즉각적으로 사용한다고 보면 된다. 아이템을 얻으면 어디에 써야할지 바로 감이 올 거다. 또 퍼즐의 힌트가 직관적이고, 눈에 잘 띄어서 놓치기 힘들다.

[h2]Предисловие[/h2]
D: The Game – это одна из тех игр, которая вызвала бурю эмоций и разногласий среди игроков и критиков. Выпущенная в середине 90-х годов, она смело шагнула в неизведанные территории игрового дизайна и повествования. Этот проект нельзя просто отложить в сторону, несмотря на его недостатки, поскольку игра является революционной и заслуживает внимания.

[h2]Сюжет[/h2]
Сюжет захватывает с первых минут. История начинается с амнезии главного героя — классического, но по-прежнему эффективного приёма для создания интриги. Введение создаёт ощущение загадки, и у игрока появляется желание разобраться в происходящем. Однако по мере продвижения игра теряет свою глубину, а финал, который должен был стать кульминацией, оказывается поспешным и недостаточно проработанным, оставляя чувство неудовлетворённости.

[h2]Геймплей[/h2]
Геймплей предлагает нечто большее, чем просто решение головоломок и борьбу за выживание. Это интерактивная история, вдохновлённая кинематографом. Визуальная стилистика и кинематографическая подача впечатляют, особенно с учётом года выхода игры. Однако динамики и напряжения, характерных для жанра хоррора, не хватает, что превращает игру в более спокойное приключение. К сожалению, в последней главе игра теряет своё кинематографическое очарование, погружая игрока в длительное и монотонное прохождение.

I did end up playing two times to get to the end, but that was because I got about an hour and a half in and it was lunch time, and my wife does not like me to miss lunch time even by one minute so I had to quit. I don't know if I'd have made it through or not, but on my next play through I had no difficulties finishing the game. There were a few moments when I thought, I should look up what to do next so I don't have to watch any more painfully slow animations, but I persevered and solved the game on my own.

Naturally the biggest complaint for this game is going to be how slowly Laura moves. Every misstep is painful because you have to watch an animation that could have been avoided. If this were a brand new game no one would play it, but as an anthropological view into video game history it is quite fascinating. D is a 1995 spooky-style FMV adventure game by Kenji Eno, sort of an enfant terrible of the gaming industry for his time (he passed in 2013 due to heart failure - peace be upon him). D places you in the shoes of Laura Harris, a high school(? maybe it was college) student who investigates a hospital after learning that her father went on a murder spree and locked himself inside. Once inside the hospital she finds it's somehow turned into a mansion, and the game starts from there. The pacing of D's story is a bit strange, and not entirely satisfying. Over the course of the game you get flashbacks to a moment in Laura's childhood, with each new flashback revealing more of the scene. Additionally you'll occasionally see a phantom-like illusion of your father's face, cryptically pleading for you to go back before "it's too late". There are two different endings to get - good and bad - and the ending you get depends on whether or not you use a certain item at the climactic encounter. I got the bad ending. Oops!

D came out at a time when CD-ROMs were still sexy (Myst having legitimized its viability as a gaming format), and FMVs weren't met with weary sighs. However D goes a step beyond Myst's relatively static world and includes a wealth of pre-rendered CG cutscenes (courtesy of Amiga 4000 work stations), and even actions like walking down a hallway, for example, are animated as if from a first-person perspective. As a result D was released on a whopping three discs while lasting roughly 90 minutes, all the more fascinating when you consider Final Fantasy VII had the same number of discs with 40 hours of gameplay. D received positive reception for its animation, story, and atmosphere, and Nintendo fanboys were thoroughly stumped as they were stuck playing cringe 2D crap like Yoshi's Island and Chrono Trigger.

Sadly time hasn't been kind to D, and the problems it had in 1995 are only exacerbated today. That said, the graphics still have a sort of uncanny timelessness to them, adding to the game's surreal atmosphere rather than detracting from it. No, the faults lie with the gameplay. First off, Laura's moving speed is slow. Incredibly slow. As a result there's going to be a lot of time spent just waiting for her to get from point A to point B. Luckily the environment isn't too sprawling, meaning it's not as bad as it could be, but still, it's almost comical how slow it can be - like moving underwater, but also the water is molasses. It may be a pretty large obstacle to overcome for gamers in 2022, but after a while I think my brain adjusted to the pacing and, while it never felt normal per se, it wasn't like my brain was eating itself while waiting.

As you may have figured by now, D's gameplay consists primarily of puzzles - "use clue X to solve puzzle Y to open door Z", that kind of structure. There's a magic pocket mirror that will show you which screen you should currently be at, but it breaks after three uses. The puzzles are pretty simple, though there were two that temporarily stumped me as I was overthinking it way too hard. Nothing made me stop and think "wow, that was clever!" but it's never cryptic in the way older adventure games could be, and I think I would rather take "too easy" over completely baffling developer logic. The most action D has is a quick-time event that occurs late game.

As mentioned before, you can complete D in around 90 minutes. There are no save points and the game has to be beaten under 2 hours lest you get a game over. Sadly I was unaware of this, and I lost my first playthrough about 2/3 in since I tabbed out of the game to chat, check forums, get something to eat, etc. As far as I know the pause screen doesn't even stop the timer. Luckily the answers to puzzles aren't arbitrarily gated, so as long as you remember the solutions and get the keys you need, you can speed up the beginning quite a bit. I beat the game on my second playthrough.

D isn't particularly good "as a game", but I still found it enjoyable. It felt like a game as developed by someone whose sole knowledge of video games came from watching his college dormmate play Myst for fifteen minutes. This, of course, is hyperbole, as Eno had prior experience developing (and composing for) games, but there's still something kind of special to the whole experience. D was Warp's first major project (their previous games being small-time 3DO/PS1 releases), and it went on to push a million units in Japan. As the story goes, Eno was pissed off Sony didn't print enough copies to keep up with the preorders for the PS1 port, so much so that he stated publicly at a Sony event that he would publish exclusively with Sega from that point forward. Additionally, Eno was afraid that certain scenes in D would be cut out due to censorship, so he developed the scenes in question without anyone's knowledge and sent a "clean" copy of the game for review, later swapping out the uncensored version when submitting it to Acclaim (remember those guys?)

So yeah, if you've read this far and feel intrigued, give D a try. It's absolutely Not For Everyone™ but if you like weird Japanese crap then you might get a kick out of it.

D is a fascinating look at a short lived era of video games that has long been dead. If you play this game without mentally putting yourself in the early to mid 90s, you will hate this game. The interactivity is barely there, what little voice acting there is does not hold up to today's standards, and the pre-rendered CG graphics are incredibly outdated. If you can, however, look at this game for what it is, and appreciate how groundbreaking it was in 1995, you could get a surprising amount out of this game. This game is certainly not for everyone, but I do genuinely love this game, and I think anyone with a PC who plays games should try it at least once, it certainly doesn't cost a lot to do so (unless you want to buy it for consoles).

D: The Game’s history is congruent with the history of its developers, Warp, a relative newcomer in the gaming industry. Having previously been hot off of developing tie-in games for older consoles, Kenji Eno wanted to create a title that was revolutionary. While it wasn’t their first game chronologically, D: The Game was the first HUGE title due to his ambitions and cartridge costs, and went to the 3DO company. Truth be told, the actual development wasn’t exactly a super huge development, as it only had around seven other people give or take helping create the game. The game originally didn’t even have a storyline at first, the gameplay being developed first before Kenji would go about creating the story, which ended up being boring to him personally. Wanting to include flashy violence and themes of cannibalism into the game, he had purposely submitted his masters late and hand delivered it with the more violent version instead of the clean version to bypass the censorship boards which I felt was a solid move on his part to give the game more flair. I’m not personally sure of any other history than what was shown before, as any other information just seems to revolve around Kenji Eno himself along with his struggles to get into the gaming industry as this title was one that he was making or breaking his career on. My experience with the game mainly comes from those old gaming lists from ScrewAttack and the early days of Youtube, learning about the history of D along with other old school titles like Phantasmagoria and Dark Seed. Later on, I had found the game on Steam and bought it, trying it once around three years ago before stopping due to a frustrating puzzle and leaving it a scathing review. However, I’ve been streaming horror games for a friend of mine every saturday and having recently just beaten The Alien Cube, this game was next on the list as a sort of closure statement, one that I felt that perhaps I needed to close the chapter on before playing the game’s sequel, D2, in the future via Dreamcast. 

For Plot and more, go here: https://www.backloggd.com/u/gamemast15r/review/1893214/

Starting with the gameplay, I’ll start by repeating a lot of what I said in my last log: this game drove me up the wall with some of it's mechanics, by mechanics I mean pulling a frustrating slot machine to match numbers up and also spinning a wheel for ten minutes trying to figure out what the hell I'm supposed to do. Other puzzles include a gear one which requires precise movements and a very simple one involving looking at constellations and matching them up with nearby statues by pressing colored buttons. They’re few and far between but can range from okay to frustrating, with the most confusing of them all being the elevator, which I got stuck on last time. The layout of the elevator is that there are twelve floors, and each time you spin the wheel it brings you up one floor and this confused me not because I don’t know how to count, but because I counted one floor more than I needed to when pulling the wheel. The only other bit of actual gameplay involves searching your environment and interacting with things VERY slowly and a combat section with a Knight that requires one button press quick time events (remember Left, Right, Left, Space Bar) to grab a sword. So what’s the exact frustration of the game? You only have two real time hours to beat the game, or it’s basically game over and you'll get one with no guide as it's kind of built for trial and error and collaborating with buddies. When the game is exceedingly slow with doing movements, how do you function in the game? Number one is by using a walkthrough (just know that during the statues, do the blue one before the green one), though the second is knowing the controls.

The Arrow Keys allow you to move around
The i button opens up your inventory
Spacebar is to interact

So now that you know that, I also want to point out that a lot of times, it takes a little while to judge the distance to both the objects you’re about to examine as well as go through the animations to actually do it. It’s really awkward and slow, though this adds to the nerve wracking feeling of attempting to complete this game in around two hours. I had completed it in around forty minutes to an hour I believe, and you could at least skip two steps if you know the statue colors beforehand to go there. Speaking of slow paced and stressful, the game’s atmosphere exceeds at creating a slower paced kind of unintentionally cheesy horror movie vibe that I appreciate and respect a fu  c kt on. The environments are varied and look creepy, with numerous objects that you look at have the chance to deliver a little creepy moment or give a surrealist flashback to some horrible stuff. Graphically the game originally came out on the 3DO, so of course it’s going to be lower on the polygon scale and less realistic. I’ve never been bothered by older graphics, if anything I simp for them and appreciate the older style. The cutscenes are admittedly blurry but follow through with some funny looking animations, mostly revolving around Laura screaming silently but with her mouth open like an old Whitest Kids U’Know skit that made me unintentionally giggle. D: The Game was a success in Japan, apparently selling over one million copies and drawing a cult fan base to the game’s eccentric nature, enough so that the game got a director’s cut release for the 3DO titled D’s Diner: Director’s Cut. However, for the Playstation Port it sort of became a huge disaster for the relations between Kenji Eno and Sony themselves due to Sony manufacturing well below the amount of units that Kenji would’ve liked. This would lead to him revealing an exclusive partnership with Sega for Warp’s future games…at a Sony Playstation event. Hilariously ballsy in hindsight, he had also originally planned to have the President of Sega appear at the event and give over 1,000 Sega Saturns out for blind people as well. However, according to Eno himself, he was apparently protected by a Sony Executive and let off the hook before going on to create spiritual successors Enemy Zero and D2 with their virtual actress Laura. As for Kenji Eno personally, the game succeeded well enough to help him and his newly married wife afford a better life for themselves, as well as give the rest of the developers of Warp their first success for being newer developers. I don’t know how well it sold personally in the U.S., but my second playthrough this time around had me appreciating this game A LOT more than I did previously. The story is simple even if I can poke holes through it, the sound design is goofy and graphically/atmospherically it’s this unintentionally funny horror game with frustrating game design. However, I also have a soft spot for old school gaming and media projects in general, with D: The Game being one of those I had a soft spot for a long time. I went from purely hating it and rating it amongst my least favorite games to being a title that I felt was average, but also an experiment that I can respect and appreciate for what it is. Does it hold up as well as it did before? Not really, no. Will I ever play this game again? Probably not, the 5 hours I have in it is only to leave it on for Steam Trading Cards. Is this game worth your money? If you want to experience old gaming history, yes as well as if you have a lot of patience. Otherwise, just watch a Youtube playthrough or something.

[i]D[/i] was everywhere in its day, the dawn of the 3D era, and many of the reviewers here are zeroed in on its historical import.  I think two aspects are of particular note regarding its success.  One, though the 3D graphics are limited (but quite good for the time), the game really illustrates how far knowledge of the language of film  -  editing, timing, shot composition  -  can go in making even a primitive 3D environment effective.  [i]D[/i] feels leaps and bounds over its contemporaries even though it's not really that much more advanced technologically.  Two, though visionary director Kenji Eno's prediction of "digital actors" appearing in different roles from game to game didn't come true, his focus on his main character and her range of expression adds life where none exists in lesser titles.  Eno gives the proceedings time to breathe, allows for reactions of astonishment and befuddlement and frustration and reflection from the heroine, and events seem more natural, relatable, and human for it.  They go a long way in helping to tell a story largely without words.

The game does still work, I think, provided you give some latitude for the two-hour time limit and don't mind investing in a scouting-out playthrough if you're coming in cold.  There's genuine tension and atmosphere, and the end of the bug flashbacks is a heck of a reveal.

Comprei por mera curiosidade e pelo fato de estar custando 1 real. É engraçado pensar que na versão de PS1 esse jogo veio em 3 discos separados, explicado pelo fato de que, apesar de poder ser completado em menos de 1 hora, o jogo é composto inteiramente por cutscenes em FMV. Laura, a protagonista, é controlada inteiramente pelas setas do teclado e mais 2 botões. Você só aponta para onde quer ir e uma cutscene dela andando é exibida, como se fosse um antepassado distante de Killer7.
No seu inventário ela carrega um relógio de bolso e se, a qualquer momento do jogo, os ponteiros indicarem meia-noite em ponto se prepare pra um game over. Isso coloca o jogador sobre um limite de tempo estrito de 2 horas para finalizar a aventura, sem contar com nenhum checkpoint ou save. De início isso pode soar um tanto intimidador, mas o jogo é tão curto que se você souber o que está fazendo é possível completá-lo sem nunca ter que se preocupar em sequer checar o relógio.
Por outro lado, se você não sabe o que está fazendo, as coisas vão adquirir um ar de frustração bem rapidamente. D já tem quase 30 anos de idade e as marcas da velhice estão por todos os lados. Mesmo depois de zerá-lo eu ainda não entendo muito bem qual a lógica de boa parte de sua progressão funciona. A maior parte do jogo consiste apenas em Laura tropeçando pelos cantos entrando em cômodos novos, se deparando com uma porta trancada, apenas para ter que voltar atrás e encontrar algum item perdido dentro de uma gaveta ou na mão de um cadáver. 
Se isso não soa engajante pra você então, bem... mesmo por 1 real não vale a pena. A história faz pouquíssimo sentido, os puzzles fazem pouquíssimo sentido e tirando o charme estético que o jogo adquiriu com seus ambiciosos gráficos 3D dos anos 90 ele é tão raso quanto um daqueles jogos de PC  educativos pra criança jogar em creche.

D is a very important piece in horror video game history. Though it is grossly dated by today's standards of gameplay design, D represented a mayor leap in what could be achieved in terms of horror story telling in videogames.
This version of the game is the DOS version emulated via DOSbox which can be tweaked to offer a decent experience.
If you're not thrilled by the prospect of having to play a slow paced, puzzle solving game made entirely of low res FMVs, perhaps it would be wise to stay away from it. If, however, all of those things hit the spot, jump in!

Как можно догадаться по скриншотам, D продается на Steam в расчете на любопытных исследователей эпохи 90-х, желающих лично прикоснуться к древним артефактам игровой индустрии, а также на аудиторию геймеров зрелого возраста, когда-то фанатевших по ней в детстве. На сегодняшний день играть в D не слишком увлекательно, ничего кроме смеха местный "хоррор" не вызывает, а геймдизайнерские решения вроде отсутствия сохранений, непропускаемых роликов и и наступления game over'а ровно через два часа после старта новой игры сперва удивляют, а потом жутко фрустрируют.

Технически проект представляет собой FMV-квест, в котором вместо живых актеров используется неплохая по меркам игровой индустрии середины 90-х гг. трехмерная графика. Геймплей заключается в перемещении по не слишком объемным комнатам, в которых игрока регулярно запирают по сюжету, решению то простых, то непонятных головоломок, нажатию кнопки "Пробел" в одних нужных местах (для поднятия предметов) и кнопки "i"  в других нужных местах (для открытия инвентаря и их использования). Короче говоря, перед нами старенькое "интерактивное кинцо", выпущенное еще до эпохи, когда жанр вышел в мейнстрим - трейлер обещает интригующий сюжет, но, в отличие от графики, из-за своей бессвязности он вряд ли мог кого-то впечатлить даже в середине 90-х.

История начинается с того, что директор госпиталя внезапно совершает массовое убийство, баррикадируется в здании, а заодно берет в заложники всех, кто в нем находился. Его дочь Лора, узнав о случившемся из телерепортажа, решает поиграть в детектива и самостоятельно выяснить что к чему. Без особых проблем проникнув внутрь госпиталя (вроде как оцепленного полицией), Лора практически сразу натыкается на загадочную материю, которая поглощает ее и переносит в готический замок (так точно, о госпитале в этой игре больше никто и не вспомнит). Там героиня первым делом встречается с духом отца, который, во-первых, сообщает, что девушка попала в реальность, созданную его разумом, а во-вторых  настоятельно рекомендует эту реальность покинуть. Поскольку дух папки забыл объяснить, как именно ее можно "покинуть", и поскольку входная дверь в замок оказывается закрытой, бедной Лоре ничего не остается, кроме как слоняться по всему зданию в поисках ключей, загадочных механизмов да артефактов (впрочем, у игрока для этих целей всегда есть Alt+F4 - возможно, именно на это отец и намекал).

Мягко скажем, в сюжетном плане D больше похожа на "хоррор", написанный десятилетним ребенком - если вы желаете сыграть в нее в надежде на хорошую историю, не тратьте время, лучше сразу оцените главный сюжетный твист: [spoiler]Лора и ее отец - потомки Дракулы, но папка, зная о грядущем превращении в вампира, не остановил процесс, желая на своем примере "узнать, как он протекает", что звучит как довольно глупая сценарная отговорка; самое забавное, что это откровение D вываливает на игрока почти сразу перед титрами, и то в виде супер-короткой экспозиции от обращающегося отца; в итоге папашка либо съедает дочь, либо ловит пулю и по-голливудски долго умирает[/spoiler]. 

Но ладно: графика устарела, геймплей рудиментарный, внятного сюжета нет - может быть, в D хотя бы приятно играть? Как уже упоминалось, здесь нельзя сохраняться - если запустили, остается лишь проходить ее до победного конца, который в любом случае наступит через два часа или меньше. Таймер истек - начинайте сначала (других способов умереть в игре, впрочем, нет); при этом здесь нет ни кнопки паузы, ни функции пропуска или перемотки одних и тех же повторяющихся роликов - любопытно, что последнее раздражает в D больше всего.

В чем проблема. Во-первых, в этих роликах наша героиня ну очень неторопливо двигается - кажется, в готическом замке с наколотыми на шипы трупами ей совсем не страшно (и это здорово бьет по атмосфере проекта). Во-вторых, как и в большинстве игр с квестовыми элементами, вам придется посещать одни и те же локации по многу раз (сначала в поиске предметов, а позже -  активных точек, где их можно применить), и каждый раз вы будете видеть один и тот же ролик о перемещении Лоры по зданию от первого лица - после третьего-четвертого просмотра каждый из них, мягко скажем, перестает впечатлять. 

И вот что еще хуже: если играть в D так, как это было задумано разработчиками (то есть, без прохождения под рукой), вы гарантированно не пройдете ее за отведенные два часа с первого раза - а это значит, что когда игра перезапустится, вам придется перепроходить ее до того момента, на котором истек таймер, чтобы найти способ продвинуться дальше. Если вы уже знаете, где что лежит и как решаются загадки, сделать это, технически, нетрудно, но... вам придется заново смотреть все те же ролики, что вы видели раньше, начиная с непропускаемой трехминутной интро-вставки! Снова черепашья ходьба по дому, снова встречи с болтливым духом отца в каждой комнате, снова затянутые флэшбеки (без поиска триггеров, которые их запускают, хорошую концовку не получить), снова длинные интермиссии при переходе из одной комнаты в другую - и все это никак не промотать! У этого проекта вообще был геймдизайнер?!.

Есть хорошая новость: если знать, куда идти и что делать, D можно проспидранить меньше, чем за час. Любопытно, что, судя по длине avi-файлов в папке с игрой, всего в проекте содержится 75 минут видео, не считая трехминутного интро-ролика и двадцатисекундной анимации для game over'а в конце второго часа (вполне ожидаемо, что по большей части это время занимает именно передвижение по замку - впрочем, некоторые комнаты здесь попросту бесполезны, а многие другие полезны только при наличии определенных предметов в инвентаре). К слову, музыки в игре маловато: важные сюжетные события в роликах могут иметь собственные коротенькие темы, но по большей части игрок будет слышать одну и ту же мелодию, которая длится 1 минуту 20 секунд (после чего повторяется). Вкупе с медлительной главной героиней, которая по глубине переживания эмоций недалеко ушла от дерева (из-за графических ограничений эпохи), приевшаяся музыка подчистую разрушает хоррорную атмосферу, а нелепые сцены вроде побега от гигантского шара а-ля Индиана Джонс или QTE-драки с ожившими железными доспехами (которые могут скинуть Лору в колодец, из которого она запросто вылазит, но не могут убить) и вовсе добавляют в D трэшевой комичности.

Вердикт: D безвозвратно устарела во всем, от графики до заскорузлых геймдизайнерских решений. Сегодня она может порадовать лишь искателей игровых древностей да бывших фанатов, заставших ее еще во времена своей юности. Не скрою, я получил от нее своего рода моральное удовлетворение - вживую увидел классику японского хоррора, важную игру для индустрии, когда-то продававшуюся для PS1 на целых трех дисках, которую кроме как на Steam сегодня с огнем не сыщешь, и так далее - но не то что бы ощутил удовольствие от самого игрового процесса. Некоторые игры плохо состариваются, и то, что эта участь постигла D, было ясно уже в 2000-х. Ожидать, что в нее станет приятнее играть когда-либо в будущем, уже не приходится.
